clue.text: Officer, single, sunk in depression

indicators.note: something sunk in a hollow sits down inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a col is a dip or pass between mountain peaks
single means lone, on one's own

explanation.surface: An unmarried army officer is suffering from low spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' reads as low spirits, but here it is the mountain sense: a dip or pass in a ridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonel is a senior army rank, so an officer.

clue.text: Coach — it crashes, out of control

indicators.note: crashes suggests a smash, so the letters of coach and it are broken up

explanation.surface: A runaway coach crashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaotic means in complete disorder.

clue.text: Short article from abroad, coming to the point

parts.note: la is the French feminine definite article
a cone tapers to a point, so conical comes to a point

explanation.surface: A brief foreign piece gets straight to the point.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconical, like laconic, means terse in speech, from the curt Spartans of Laconia.

clue.text: Component of petard can hoist the engineer

indicators.note: hoist lifts the word up, reading it backwards in a down entry

parts.note: a tin is a can
RE is the Royal Engineers

explanation.surface: Echoes 'hoist with his own petard': the engineer blown up by his own bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: A petard was an early explosive charge; nitre (saltpetre) is in gunpowder.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitre, potassium nitrate, is a key ingredient of gunpowder, which filled a petard.

clue.text: Murder — deceased carried only one pound

indicators.note: carried means holding something inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: late means deceased, as in 'the late king'
I is the Roman numeral one
a quid is British slang for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: A murder victim had just a pound on them.
explanation.definitionFit: To liquidate a person is to kill them, a euphemism for murder.

clue.text: With an obsession, Teddy can inspire fear

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for a noun: a thing that can inspire fear

parts.note: a bug is a craze or obsession, as in 'the travel bug'
a teddy is a teddy bear, the toy

explanation.surface: A child fixated on a cuddly toy might find it frightening.
explanation.definitionFit: A bugbear was originally a goblin used to scare children, hence something dreaded.

clue.text: A couple to stay

explanation.surface: Two people decide to remain.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a pair, of game birds for example; a brace also props or supports something.

clue.text: One found in bird book, when looking up

definitions.text: One found in bird book, when looking up

indicators.note: found in places the numeral inside the bird

parts.note: a gull is a seabird
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: looking up turns the word upwards, read backwards in a down entry

parts.note: a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher spots a species while glancing up from a field guide.
explanation.definitionFit: The guillemot is a black-and-white seabird of the auk family.

clue.text: Woman about to approve produce

indicators.note: about means around, so the woman goes round the other piece

parts.note: Eve is the first woman in Genesis
to OK something is to approve it

explanation.surface: A woman is on the point of signing off some produce.
explanation.definitionFit: To evoke is to call up or bring forth a feeling or memory.

clue.text: From a castle at Rye, perhaps, to mean tenements

parts.note: the rook is the chess piece also called a castle

indicators.note: perhaps hints the word could be otherwise, so the letters of Rye are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grand castle at the Sussex town of Rye is said to mean slum housing.
explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a small town in East Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: A rookery was a crowded slum of run-down tenements, like a colony of nesting rooks.

clue.text: Meeting Frenchman lacking in charm

indicators.note: lacking says one piece goes without the stated letter, so it is taken away

parts.note: a mascot is a lucky charm
M is short for monsieur, a Frenchman

explanation.surface: A meeting with a Frenchman who has no charm.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is a famous English racecourse, and a race fixture is called a 'meeting'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a race meeting held each June at the Berkshire course.

clue.text: Low Sunday, as it were — first of days in low surroundings

parts.note: quasi is Latin for 'as it were', 'as if'

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the other, the low surroundings

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do

indicators.note: first of means only the opening letter of days is used

explanation.surface: A churchgoer notes the quiet Sunday, its first day spent in humble surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surroundings' rounds off the picture: MOO surrounds D. 'Low' changes sense between the definition and the cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sunday after Easter is Quasimodo Sunday, from its Latin introit beginning 'Quasi modo'.

clue.text: Coloured man from Morocco

explanation.surface: A man of colour comes from North Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangerine is a deep orange shade; a Tangerine is a native of Tangier, the Moroccan port.

clue.text: Subject of false report, for instance, that's put about

parts.note: a lie is a false statement

indicators.note: put about means turned round, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: EG, exempli gratia, means for instance

explanation.surface: Someone is the target of an untrue rumour that has been spread around.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege can be a vassal owing feudal service, so a subject of a lord.

clue.text: Merger of firms concluded with a drink

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm
a second company, as the merger joins two firms

explanation.surface: Two companies seal their merger over a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merger of firms' gives two COs side by side; 'concluded with' adds A at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot chocolate beverage.

clue.text: Evasion — the French have no right to the ball

indicators.note: no right means the R is dropped from the French verb

parts.note: avoir is the French verb to have
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: French dodgers are barred from the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Avoidance is the act of keeping away from something, so evasion.

clue.text: Current society escort

parts.note: AC is alternating current
company means society, companionship

explanation.surface: A fashionable socialite's escort.
explanation.definitionFit: To accompany someone is to go along with them as an escort.

clue.text: Unbelievable profit, we're — told

parts.note: said aloud, profit is prophet: a seer whom no one believed, from Greek myth

explanation.surface: We hear of an implausibly large gain.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek legend the Trojan princess was cursed to prophesy truly but never be believed. The dash is an OCR artefact; the page prints none.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassandra was the Trojan seer fated to have her warnings ignored.

clue.text: My rest may get disturbed by lack of balance

indicators.note: get disturbed means thrown into disorder, so the letters of my rest may are mixed

explanation.surface: My sleep may be interrupted by feeling unsteady.
explanation.definitionFit: Asymmetry is the absence of symmetry or proportion between parts.

clue.text: Anyone who likes can give me collars

indicators.note: the letters of the words that follow can give, when rearranged, a new phrase

explanation.surface: Whoever wants to can hand me collars.
explanation.definitionFit: A competition open to all comers admits anybody who wishes to enter.

clue.text: Monk put up school in compound

indicators.note: put up raises the word, read backwards in a down entry

parts.note: a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist monk
a gam is a school of whales

explanation.surface: A monk is lodged at a school in a walled enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: An amalgam is a mixture or blend, especially of mercury with another metal.

clue.text: Arrange to meet in Coventry station

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words Coventry station

explanation.surface: Two people agree to rendezvous at a Midlands railway station.
explanation.definitionFit: To tryst is to make a secret date, as lovers do.

clue.text: Half go bust a number of times

parts.note: ten is a number
a business that folds goes bust

explanation.surface: Half the firms collapse again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' tells you each piece is half of the answer: one half is 'go bust', the other 'a number'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenfold means ten times as much or as many.

clue.text: A loaf in the van

parts.note: loaf is slang for head, as in 'use your loaf'

explanation.surface: A loaf of bread is in the delivery van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your loaf' is British rhyming slang: loaf of bread = head. 'Van' is short for vanguard, the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The van is the vanguard, so being in the van is being out in front.

clue.text: With equal stakes in the Robert Louis Centre

indicators.note: Centre keeps only the middle, so the outer letters of the surname are dropped

parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island

explanation.surface: Bets at a centre named after the Scottish author.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove ST from the front and ON from the end of STEVENSON to leave its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Evens is betting odds of one to one, where the stake equals the winnings.

clue.text: Comedian chronicled by Hornung?

parts.note: a comedian is one who cracks jokes, a crack-man; Hornung wrote of Raffles, an amateur safebreaker

explanation.surface: A stand-up comic features in the stories of E. W. Hornung.
explanation.walkthrough: E. W. Hornung wrote the Raffles stories; the first collection is 'The Amateur Cracksman', about a gentleman burglar.
explanation.definitionFit: A cracksman is a burglar or safebreaker, which Raffles was.

clue.text: Shy girl, without sex appeal

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letters for sex appeal are removed

parts.note: Charity is a girl's name
it was 1920s slang for sex appeal, as in the 'It girl'

explanation.surface: A bashful young woman lacks allure.
explanation.definitionFit: Chary means cautious or wary, so reluctant or shy.

clue.text: Potassium and nitrogen have become familiar

parts.note: K is the chemical symbol for potassium
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen
to own is to have

explanation.surface: Two chemical elements have become well acquainted.
explanation.definitionFit: Something known is recognised or familiar.

clue.text: Country, about to invade England, diverted

indicators.note: to invade is to go into, so one piece enters the other
diverted means sent another way, so the letters of England are rearranged

parts.note: RE means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A nation is set to invade England, which is thrown off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' tempts you to look for a nation England might fear; it is just the definition, and 'about' supplies the two letters that go into the reshuffled England.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenland is a large Arctic island and autonomous territory.

clue.text: Top garden party?

parts.note: a garden is outside, out of doors
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: Asking what the best kind of garden party is.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the loose 'garden' for OUT: an outdoor do is a garden party.
explanation.definitionFit: To outdo someone is to surpass or beat them.

clue.text: The flower is within my grasp

indicators.note: within places the flower inside the other word

parts.note: an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A gardener says the bloom is in reach.
explanation.definitionFit: Mastery of a subject is full command or grasp of it.

clue.text: Cross when anodyne is misused

indicators.note: misused means used wrongly, so the letters of anodyne are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone gets angry when a painkiller is abused.
explanation.definitionFit: Being annoyed is being irritated or angry.
